title: Quibi's Leaders Shut It Down While There Was Money Left to Return
dek: In October 2020, six months after launch, Quibi's founder and chief executive chose to close the service and hand back roughly $350 million rather than spend it.

story.founder: Jeffrey Katzenberg (founder) and Meg Whitman (chief executive)
story.event: Closing a short-form streaming service six months after launch and returning remaining cash to investors
story.summary: Quibi, a mobile-only service of short premium shows founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg and run by Meg Whitman, raised about $1.75 billion and launched on 6 April 2020 as pandemic lockdowns kept people at home. On 21 October 2020, with about $350 million still in the bank, they announced they would wind it down and return cash to shareholders rather than raise more; the service ended on 1 December 2020, about 200 staff lost their jobs, and Roku bought rights to 75 of its shows in January 2021.
paragraphs: On 21 October 2020, Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman finished telling Quibi's investors that the company would close, posted an open letter, and prepared for a virtual town hall with most of their roughly 200 staff. Quibi, a paid service of short shows made for phones, had launched on 6 April, in the middle of the shutdowns that began in mid-March. Katzenberg had conceived it after selling DreamWorks Animation and recruited Whitman, a former eBay chief, to run it. Investors, every major Hollywood studio among them, had put in about $1.75 billion.

Everything had been designed for moments on the move, and, as Katzenberg put it, suddenly nobody was on the move. Over the summer, Whitman said, they tried free trials of different lengths, marketed individual shows instead of the platform, and tested a different model in Australia. None of it changed the answer. To reach scale they would need to raise far more money early in 2021, and they did not think their numbers would support it. CNBC reported about 500,000 subscribers against a first-year projection of more than 7 million.

About $350 million remained, enough, Whitman said, to keep operating for a significant time. They chose not to spend it. "Most entrepreneurs just keep on going because they literally run out of money," she told Deadline. Katzenberg said carrying on would only burn more money with nothing to show for it, which, out of respect for those who had put up the capital, would be irresponsible. Their letter offered two explanations without choosing: the idea was not strong enough to stand alone, or the timing was wrong. They suspected both, and ended with "a profound apology for disappointing you".

The service went dark on 1 December 2020, and about 200 people lost their jobs; reports said they would receive severance. The ending was not tidy everywhere: a Quibi drama crew in Kyiv, told to stop, kept filming while its producers looked for money to finish. In January 2021 Roku bought rights to 75 Quibi shows, reportedly for well under $100 million, and Katzenberg said he was glad the stories had found a new home.

quote.text: Confirm thy word, and keep faith with him; and at all seasons thou shalt find what thou needest. Many have reckoned a loan as a windfall, and have given trouble to those that helped them.
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira warns against treating what others entrust to you as a windfall. Quibi's leaders, still able to keep spending, gave back what remained instead. Because most of the $1.75 billion had already gone, the line praises their choice and measures it at the same time.

reflection: Stopping early is usually described as a failure of nerve. Whitman described it the other way round: the common move would have been to keep going until the money ran out, and choosing to stop while something could still be handed back was, she said, a matter of maturity.

You may never hold hundreds of millions for other people, but you do hold their trust: a colleague's time, your family's patience, your own energy on a long week. Now and then it is worth asking what you could still hand back if you stopped today, and whether that amount is quietly shrinking.
invitation: Name one commitment you are keeping alive mainly because stopping would feel like failure. Write down what you could still hand back if you stopped this month, and decide nothing more today.

cross_checks.claim: On 21 October 2020 Katzenberg and Whitman announced in an open letter that Quibi would wind down and return cash to shareholders.
About $350 million remained when the decision was announced.
The letter gave two possible reasons, the idea or the timing, and suspected a combination.
Quibi launched in early April 2020 and the service ended on 1 December 2020.
Roku acquired rights to 75 Quibi shows in January 2021.

research_notes: Money raised disagrees across reports: $1.75 billion (AP via CBS and News4Jax, CNBC's article body, Engadget, Deadline's December report, Tubefilter 2021); 'over $1.7 billion' (Deadline's interview); $1.8 billion (CFO.com citing Crunchbase, Tubefilter 2020, Business Insider); 'nearly $2 billion' (The Hollywood Reporter, CNBC's summary); Fox Business gives $1 billion, apparently the first round. The story uses $1.75 billion. Cash remaining: Deadline says around $350 million; Engadget cites the WSJ's report that Katzenberg told investors about $350 million remained; Whitman told CNBC there was 'at least $350 million' and that 'much more' would be returned after the wind-down. The final amount returned to investors was not found in a source that loads, so the story says only that they chose to hand back what remained. Subscribers: Quibi did not publish figures; CNBC reported about 500,000 subscribers against a projection of more than 7 million; Deadline (1 December) mentions 500,000 or so sign-ups; Sensor Tower's 9.6 million app installs are not subscribers and are not used. Whitman's role: CNBC issued a correction that she was CEO and not a co-founder, so the story calls Katzenberg the founder and Whitman the chief executive he recruited. Severance is reported by Rolling Stone (citing the WSJ) and attributed as 'reports said'. The story's reasons for the failure are only those Katzenberg and Whitman gave themselves (the idea, the timing, the pandemic's effect on on-the-go viewing); investor criticism reported by Deadline is not used. The Roku price is the WSJ's report via Tubefilter and is attributed as 'reportedly'. The Ben Sira passage concerns lending and repaying a neighbour; Quibi's investors held equity rather than loans, so it is applied by analogy.
